newsitem.title: USA: Ranariddh, in U.S., promises no Khmer Rouge links.
newsitem.headline: Ranariddh, in U.S., promises no Khmer Rouge links.

text.p: Cambodia's Prince Norodom Ranariddh promised the United States on Friday that he would not bring the reviled Khmer Rouge guerrilla group into government if he is restored to power.
"I do not have any interest to flirt with the Khmer Rouge," the prince, ousted by his co-premier Hun Sen, told reporters after meeting Undersecretary of State Thomas Pickering.
State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns quoted Ranariddh as telling Pickering: "I have nothing to do with the Khmer Rouge and I will not bring them into positions of power."
Burns welcomed the assurance "because we firmly oppose any participation by the Khmer Rouge in Cambodian politics."

The United States has condemned Hun Sen for initiating last week's fighting that ended the fragile coalition and tipped the Southeast Asian nation back toward civil war. But it also has expressed concern over a "flirtation" between Ranariddh's political party and members of the Khmer Rouge.

The Cambodia fighting exploded weeks after reports that the notorious Khmer Rouge leader Pol Pot had been apprehended by his own men, prompting contacts between the capital Phnom Penh and the remnants of the Khmer Rouge inside Cambodia.

Before the United Nations-brokered peace settlement of 1991, forces associated with Ranariddh were linked in a loose guerrilla coalition fighting with the Khmer Rouge against the Vietnamese-backed Hun Sen government in Phnom Penh.

Ranariddh told reporters, "I do not need the Khmer Rouge. The Khmer Rouge are close to completely disintegrating." He accused Hun Sen of initiating contacts with one former leader of the group, Ieng Sary, who defected earlier this year.
More than one million people died under the brutal Maoist Khmer Rouge rule from 1975 to 1979.
Ranariddh said what he wanted from Washington now was "a signal sent to Phnom Penh that the United States of America will not accept a regime issuing from a coup d'etat."

He welcomed Washington's decision on Thursday to suspend aid to Cambodia for 30 days but said this should be an indefinite freeze until a legitimate government is restored in Phnom Penh reflecting the 1993 election.

Ranariddh implicitly conceded it would be virtually impossible, however, to restore the old coalition government, calling instead for cooperation between the parties just to arrange elections that are scheduled for next year.
Ranariddh, son of King Sihanouk, one of Asia's wiliest and longest-surviving leaders, said he wanted to meet Hun Sen but believed it was not safe for him to return to Phnom Penh now.
He said had offered to meet Hun Sen in Beijing, where Sihanouk is having medical treatment, but that was rejected.

Ranariddh said he would travel shortly to Indonesia, which played a key role in bringing about the 1991 peace accords, and would meet a team of ASEAN foreign ministers who also plan to talk with Sihanouk and Hun Sen in search of a settlement.
U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright is due to travel to Malaysia at the end of July for meetings with ASEAN foreign ministers at which Cambodia will be a major topic.

Ranariddh said if diplomatic efforts and economic sanctions failed to force a return to the arrangements worked out under the 1991 agreements, "we will have to think ... of resistance." But he said he did not want to talk of fighting because "the people of Cambodia have suffered too long."
Forces of the two sides were still fighting outside the capital on Friday, with engagements reported near Siem Reap, close to the famed temple of Angkor Wat.
Congressional leaders also met Ranariddh and assured him of their support, backing an indefinite suspension of aid.

House International Relations Committee Chairman Benjamin Gilman of New York and Senate Foreign Relations Committee Chairman Jesse Helms of North Carolina sent President Bill Clinton a letter saying: "This military coup must be reversed and the administration must play a leading role."
